catalog_quote: Kharia has no distinctive tones or accent. Nevertheless, as will be shown in the following pages, the pitch pattern plays an important role in defining the phonological word in Kharia. ... All contentive morphemes in the language, as well as adpositions and a few other elements such as the reciprocal marker kol (6.3.5), show a “low→high” (LH) pitch pattern. ... In polysyllabic morphemes the final syllable has a high tone and the first syllable either has a low tone or drops to a low point before rising again. In monosyllabic morphemes we find a rising pitch. [p. 36] There is no expiratory accent in Kharia and any syllable of the contentive morpheme may be more “prominent” with respect to intensity (cf. Rehberg, 2003: 24ff. and 53ff. (tables)). Although the intensity does tend to be highest in bisyllabic contentive morphemes on the last syllable, where the high tone is found, it is quite often the case that the first syllable is pronounced with a higher intensity than the last syllable, and often the two syllables are approximately equal in terms of intensity. On the other hand, the pitch pattern described above is ALWAYS found in the contentive morpheme.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kharia (khar1287) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's single title-hit, Glottolog's 'Rehberg 1966 Phonologie des Kharia', is a mis-dated record of Kerstin Rehberg's 2003 Osnabrück MA thesis (Peterson 2011: 36 fn. 7 and Horo & Anderson 2022: 317 both cite it as 2003, MA Thesis, Universität Osnabrück); Second-hand, Rehberg posits a non-distinctive initial low-tone pitch accent. The best first-hand statement actually read is Peterson 2011: 35-36 (page scan held by the project): 'Kharia has no distinctive tones or accent.. There is no expiratory accent in Kharia and any syllable of the contentive morpheme may be more prominent with respect to intensity'; word-level prosody is an obligatory LH pitch pattern (final syllable of the contentive morpheme high) that delimits the phonological word.org full-text snippets of Peterson 2008 (Routledge Munda Languages, lending-only) with the same 'no expiratory accent.. low-tone pitch begins each phonological word' wording; Horo & Anderson 2022 (JSEALS SP8, open, saved) discussing Rehberg vs. Peterson and tabulating Kharia as 'Conflicting: initial/second/final? L-pitch initial, H-pitch second/final, intensity on non-initial syllables, not yet formally investigated'; Easterday 2019 (OAPEN, saved) coding Kharia 'Word stress: No; Tone: No' from Peterson 2011. Older sources are silent (SPA 1979 digest of Biligiri 1965/Pinnow 1959: 'neither source mentions stress or accent'; LSI Jharkhand/Orissa Kharia chapters list only length and nasalization). Peterson & Maas 2009 (Morphology 19) is paywalled and not read; Peterson's Brill grammar is listed as Open Access on his Kiel CV page but Brill blocks non-browser access. Recommended coding if added: no word stress (edge-marking pitch pattern), deciding source Peterson 2011: 35-36. All downloaded material is under and.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kharia has no word stress (no distinctive accent, no expiratory/intensity accent: intensity may peak on any syllable). What is fixed is an obligatory word-level pitch contour: every contentive morpheme (and adpositions etc.) carries a low-to-high (LH) pattern, low on the first syllable and high on the final syllable (rising within a monosyllable); enclitics fall outside it, and the phonological word is defined as the stretch from one LH onset to the next LH onset or a pause. If forced into a prominence frame, the pitch peak is morpheme-final, but the author explicitly denies that this is stress or a pitch accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; Peterson (p. 44, via snippet) notes Rehberg found neither primary nor secondary accent in compounds, and in his terms each member simply shows its own LH pattern.
new_statements.exceptions: Phonological and syntactic clitics lack the LH pattern; pitch may drop off on the last syllable in isolation forms but only after peaking; words beginning with /s/ or some vowels (e.g. /o/) may start slightly higher before dipping and rising; TAM/person enclitics after a monosyllabic base not ending in a glottal stop can be incorporated into the LH pattern (p. 45 snippet). Fn. 7: Rehberg (2003: 23ff.) instead analyses a non-distinctive low-tone pitch accent on the word-initial syllable; Peterson rejects this because monosyllables (rising, no low) would then be accentless.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = contentive morpheme (semantic base) plus following enclitics; based on Praat analysis of isolated words and connected texts (Dudh Kharia speakers, Jharkhand). Sentence prosody treated separately in sec. 2.6 (pp. 46-49): declaratives relatively monotonous with gradual declination; each word-initial low pitch clearly articulated in livelier speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Peterson 2011 describes exclusively the Dudh Kharia variety (southwestern Jharkhand: Simdega/Gumla area); Dhelki Kharia not investigated. This is khar1287 at language level (no separate Glottolog dialect codes used). Peterson dates Rehberg's Osnabrück thesis to 2003 (Glottolog's record 685104 gives no reliable year).

new_statements.reading: No word stress in Kharia: no expiratory (dynamic) accent and no distinctive tone or accent. The only word-level prosody is a demarcative LH pitch pattern (low on the first syllable, high on the last syllable of the contentive morpheme) that marks the left edge of the phonological word; intensity prominence is not fixed to any syllable (tends to be final in disyllables but often initial or equal). Instrumental (Praat). Peterson explicitly rejects Rehberg's (2003) alternative of a non-distinctive initial low-tone pitch accent; Horo & Anderson (2022: 314-315) read the same data as pointing to second-syllable prominence in disyllables and call the picture 'conflicting.. not yet formally investigated'. For a catalog entry this is no-word-stress (edge-marking pitch, not culminative stress); if a placement had to be recorded from the pitch peak it would be final-syllable-of-the-morpheme (Rehberg's reading would be initial). Language identity: Dudh Kharia of Simdega district, Jharkhand = khar1287.

new_statements.quote: In the present study, I do not assume a low-tone accent in Kharia. Rather, I propose that it is the 'low — high' prosodic pattern itself which defines a phonological word in Kharia rather than a low-tone accent. Thus, each phonological word in Kharia begins with a low-tone pitch which then gradually rises throughout the remainder of the phonological word. If the word is monosyllabic, then we find a rising contour [...] There is no expiratory accent in Kharia and any syllable of the phonological word may be more 'prominent' with respect to volume (Rehberg 2003:24ff. and 53ff. (tables)).

new_statements.relation_note: Same author and the same analysis as the existing Peterson 2011 statements (no expiratory accent; LH pitch pattern defines the phonological word; any syllable may be more prominent in intensity/volume). It adds the explicit rejection of Rehberg's 2003 initial low-tone pitch accent analysis and the note that intonation is little studied. It confirms the catalog's blank-rule record should read as no word stress (edge-marking pitch, not culminative stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No expiratory (dynamic) word stress: intensity prominence can sit on any syllable of the phonological word. The only word-level prosody is a demarcative low-to-high pitch rise that starts low on the first syllable and rises to the end of the phonological word (a rising contour on monosyllables); Peterson treats this LH pattern as what defines the phonological word, not as an accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Peterson reports and rejects the alternative analysis of Rehberg (2003:23ff.): '(2003:23ff.) analysis, Kharia has a non-distinctive pitch accent, marked by a low-tone on the first syllable | of the word. After this syllable, the pitch then gradually rises on the following..' (pp. 436-437). Sec. 2.5: 'Little work has yet been done on Kharia intonation. Rehberg (2003:37ff..'. The archive.org scan is lending-only (pdf, epub, hocr all private; download and search-inside could not be reached by automated download), so the quote is assembled from overlapping public full-text-search snippets; the words between the bracketed gap (the examples rocho'b 'side' and lay 'tongue' with transcriptions) were not read in full.
new_statements.identity_note: Peterson 2008 (snippet, intro to the Kharia chapter) notes three groups called Kharia -- Dudh, D(h)elki and Hill Kharia -- 'Of these three groups, apparently only the Dudh and D(h)elki Kharia speak Kharia'. Peterson's own data (2008, 2011) are Dudh Kharia of Simdega district, Jharkhand = khar1287. Mahapatra 1976 draws on Biligiri 1965 and gives no dialect.

sources.note: 'Kharia has no distinctive tones or accent'; 'There is no expiratory accent in Kharia' (intensity may peak on any syllable); instead every contentive morpheme carries an obligatory low->high (LH) pitch pattern, final syllable H, first syllable L, monosyllables rising; this LH pattern defines the phonological word (unit from one LH onset to the next LH or pause; enclitics outside it).
